newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany blames foreigners for crime spree.
newsitem.headline: Germany blames foreigners for crime spree.

text.p: German Interior Minister Manfred Kanther said on Tuesday foreigners were mainly responsible for a wave of organised crime that has swept across the country following the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe.
Speaking at the Federal Crime Office, Kanther called on German courts and the country's 16 regional states to take bolder steps to thwart a rise in organised crime.
"We have to start showing our teeth...We have to make it clear to the criminals that this nation is determined and capable of protecting the security of its citizens," he said.

Nearly two-thirds of the criminal suspects in Germany were foreigners from 87 different nations while about one-third of the criminals were Germans. There were 50,000 criminal acts in Germany in 1985, he said.
"Foreign criminals and criminal groups play the leading role," he said. "The percentage of foreigners suspected in acts of crime is thus twice as high as the rate in general."
Kanther's speech followed a move last week by the lower house of parliament, which approved a draft law making it easier and faster to deport foreigners convicted of violence.

The bill reduces the minimum jail sentences of which a foreigner must be convicted to face expulsion, to three years from five. It also added aggravated breach of the peace to the list of crimes for which someone can be deported.

Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said the government had made many mistakes in fighting organised crime, but agreed that much of it was being governed from abroad.
"The masterminds are sitting abroad and laughing their heads off at us," Scharping told SWF1 radio. "They're collecting the money and leaving us here to deal with the damages and the victims."
Kanther said police efforts were complicated by international barriers and languages, but he criticised courts for failing to fully utilise laws already on the books.
Aside from urging Germany's neighbours to redouble efforts to stop drug smugglers and other criminals in their own lands, Kanther called for tighter control on Germany's borders.
He also urged local police forces to increase raids on construction sites, restaurants and areas where many foreigners are illegally employed thanks to organised crime bands.
